explain your day to day linux activities: I spend most of my time in the terminal, using commands like `git status` to track changes and `grep` to search for specific patterns. I also frequently use `top` or `htop` to monitor system resource utilization and identify potential bottlenecks. When working on a project, I'll often switch between multiple terminals to run concurrent processes, such as building code with `make` while running tests in another tab. To manage my workflow, I use tools like `tmux` for session management and `screen` for logging in remotely.
how do you troubleshoot high cpu utiliza: To troubleshoot high CPU utilization, I first check the system load average with `top` or `htop`. If a specific process is consuming excessive resources, I use `ps aux | grep <process_name>` to identify its PID and then run `strace -p <PID>` to analyze system calls. Next, I examine the process's resource usage with `pmap -d <PID>`. To further diagnose, I may enable kernel logging with `sysctl kern.log_level=7` and review the `/var/log/messages` file for relevant entries. If necessary, I'll restart or terminate the offending process to restore system performance.
how do you identify which process is con: To identify which process is consuming memory, use the `top` command. This will display a list of running processes and their corresponding memory usage. You can also use the `ps` command with the `-o` option to specify the output format, for example: `ps -eo pid,ppid,%mem,%cpu --sort=-%mem`. This will show you the process ID, parent process ID, memory usage, and CPU usage of each process, sorted by memory usage in descending order. Be aware that high memory usage can be a sign of a resource-intensive process or a potential memory leak.
explain the linux boot process: The Linux boot process begins with the Power-On Self-Test (POST) phase, which checks the system's hardware for any issues. If everything is okay, it loads the Master Boot Record (MBR) from the hard drive into memory and transfers control to the bootloader, typically GRUB. The bootloader then reads the kernel image from disk and passes control to it. The kernel initializes the system by loading device drivers, mounting file systems, and setting up network interfaces. Finally, it executes the `/etc/rc.d/*` scripts or systemd services to start system services.
explain systemd: Systemd is a system and service manager for Linux operating systems. It provides a replacement for System V init and other initialization systems. Systemd manages system services, such as network interfaces, databases, and web servers, by running them in the background and monitoring their status. It also handles system startup and shutdown processes. Systemd uses a hierarchical structure to manage services, with each service represented by a unit file in `/etc/systemd/system/`. The `systemctl` command is used to control systemd services.
what happens when linux boots: When Linux boots, the following events occur: (1) Power-On Self-Test (POST): checks hardware for issues. (2) Loads Master Boot Record (MBR) from hard drive into memory and transfers control to bootloader. (3) Bootloader reads kernel image from disk and passes control to it. (4) Kernel initializes system by loading device drivers, mounting file systems, and setting up network interfaces. (5) Executes `/etc/rc.d/*` scripts or systemd services to start system services.
difference between hard link and soft li: A hard link is a reference to the same inode as another file on the filesystem. It's essentially an alias for the original file, and changes made through one link affect the other. A soft link, also known as a symbolic link, is a separate entity that points to the location of another file or directory. When you delete the target of a hard link, the link itself becomes invalid; with a soft link, deleting the target breaks the link.
explain linux permissions: Linux permissions are based on three types: owner (u), group (g), and others (o). Each type has read (r), write (w), and execute (x) permissions. The `umask` value determines the default permissions for newly created files. For example, if `umask` is set to 022, new files will have `rw-r--r--` permissions. Important trade-offs include balancing security with usability: overly restrictive permissions can hinder collaboration, while too permissive settings may compromise data integrity.
how do you troubleshoot high memory util: To troubleshoot high memory utilization, run `top` or `htop`, sort by memory usage (`%MEM` column), and identify the top processes consuming memory. Use `pmap -d <pid>` to analyze a process's memory map. Check for memory leaks using `valgrind` or `memcheck`. Monitor system logs for errors related to memory allocation.
what is load average: Load Average measures the average number of processes waiting in the run queue over a specified time period (1, 5, and 15 minutes). It indicates system load and can be used to detect bottlenecks. Use `cat /proc/loadavg` or `uptime` to view current Load Average values.
what does the uptime command show: The uptime command shows the system's up time, number of users logged in, and system load averages for the past 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It also displays the total number of processes running and the number of processes sleeping or stopped.
difference between top and htop: `top` displays real-time system information, while `htop` is an interactive version with additional features like sorting, filtering, and searching. Both display process CPU usage, memory consumption, and other metrics.
difference between free and vmstat: `free` reports the total, used, and free memory, as well as swap space information. `vmstat`, on the other hand, provides detailed statistics about memory usage, including page faults, disk I/O, and CPU utilization.
how do you identify which process is con: To identify which process is consuming CPU, use `top` or `htop` and sort by CPU usage (`%CPU` column). You can also use `ps -eo pcpu,pid,comm` to display a list of processes sorted by CPU usage. Use `pstack <pid>` to analyze the call stack of a process.
explain chmod 755: `chmod 755` sets permissions for a file or directory: owner has read, write, and execute (`rwx`) permissions, group members have read and execute (`rx`) permissions, and others have read and execute (`rx`) permissions. This is a common permission set for executable files.
explain chmod 777: `chmod 777` sets permissions for a file or directory: owner has read, write, and execute (`rwx`) permissions, group members have read, write, and execute (`rwx`) permissions, and others have read, write, and execute (`rwx`) permissions. This is an insecure permission set that should be avoided.
difference between sudo and su: `sudo` allows a user to run a command with superuser privileges for a short period, while `su` switches the current user to another user account. Use `sudo` when you need temporary elevated privileges, and use `su` when you need to switch to a different user account.
explain file descriptors: File descriptors (FDs) are small integer values used by processes to refer to open files or network connections. Each FD is associated with a file descriptor table entry, which contains information about the corresponding file or connection. Use `lsof` or `netstat` to display open FDs and their corresponding files or connections.
how do you check disk usage: To check disk usage, use the `df` command. For example: `df -h` will display human-readable file system disk space usage. Be aware that high disk usage can lead to production failure modes such as slow performance and potential data loss.
what logs do you check during troublesho: During troubleshooting, check the `/var/log/syslog`, `/var/log/messages`, and `/var/log/daemon.log` logs for relevant error messages. Be cautious of security concerns when reviewing logs, especially if they contain sensitive information such as passwords or API keys.
how do you find large files: To find large files, use the `find` command with the `-size` option. For example: `find / -type f -size +100M` will search for files larger than 100 megabytes. Be aware of potential reliability concerns if this command is run on a large file system.
how do you schedule cron jobs: To schedule cron jobs, use the `crontab` command to edit the crontab file. For example: `crontab -e` will open the editor for the current user's crontab. Be aware of potential security concerns if the cron job is not properly secured.
how do you automate linux administration: To automate Linux administration, use tools such as Ansible or Puppet to manage configuration and deployment. For example: `ansible-playbook -i hosts playbook.yml` will run an Ansible playbook on a set of hosts. Be aware of potential trade-offs between automation and flexibility.
how do you troubleshoot a service that w: To troubleshoot a service that won't start, check the system logs for error messages related to the service. For example: `systemctl status <service_name>` will display the status of the service. Be aware of potential production failure modes such as slow performance or data loss if the service is critical.
difference between docker and virtual ma: Docker and Virtual Machine are both containerization platforms, but Docker uses a lightweight virtualization layer to run containers, whereas VMs use full hardware emulation. This makes Docker more efficient in terms of resource usage.
explain docker daemon: The Docker daemon is the background process that manages Docker containers and images on the host system. It listens for API requests from the `docker` command-line tool and manages container lifecycle events.
explain docker engine: Docker Engine is a software platform that provides a runtime environment for Docker containers. It includes the Docker daemon, as well as tools such as `docker-compose` and `docker-machine`. The Docker Engine manages the creation, execution, and deletion of containers on the host system.
difference between image and container: A Docker Image is a template that defines an application's environment, including dependencies and configuration. A Container is an instance of a Docker Image, which runs as a process on the host system. This means that multiple Containers can be created from the same Image.
explain docker networking: Docker networking uses a combination of the host's network stack and a virtual network to enable communication between containers. Containers can be connected to a bridge network, which allows them to communicate with each other and the host. The `docker run` command can specify a custom network using the `-net` flag.
bridge vs host networking: Bridge networking is the default mode in Docker and provides isolation between containers while still allowing communication with the host. Host networking, on the other hand, allows containers to use the host's IP address and port range, but can introduce security risks if not properly configured.
explain docker volumes: Docker volumes are directories that persist data even after a container is deleted. They can be created using `docker volume create` or by mounting an existing directory with the `-v` flag in `docker run`. Volumes provide persistence and sharing of data between containers.
explain bind mounts: Bind mounts are a type of Docker volume that mount a host directory into a container. They can be created using the `-v` flag in `docker run`, specifying the path to the host directory. Bind mounts provide direct access to host files and directories.
how do you reduce docker image size: To reduce Docker image size, use multi-stage builds with `ARG` variables to separate build-time dependencies from runtime dependencies. Use `COPY --from=stage` instead of `RUN` commands to copy artifacts between stages. Remove unnecessary packages and files using `apt-get purge` or `yum remove`. Use a smaller base image, such as `alpine`, for the final stage.
how do you debug a running container: To debug a running container, use `docker logs` to view container output, `docker exec` to run commands inside the container, and `docker inspect` to examine container metadata. Use `docker stats` to monitor resource usage and identify potential issues.
explain namespaces: Namespaces in Docker provide isolation between containers by separating their process trees, network stacks, and mount points. They can be used to prevent privilege escalation attacks and improve container security. The `docker run` command can specify a custom namespace using the `-net-namespace` flag.
explain cgroups: Cgroups in Docker provide resource isolation between containers by limiting CPU, memory, and I/O usage. They can be used to prevent resource starvation attacks and improve container security. The `docker run` command can specify custom cgroup settings using the `-cgroup` flag.
explain control plane: The Control Plane is the central component of a Kubernetes cluster, responsible for managing the state of the cluster. It consists of several components: API Server, Controller Manager, Scheduler, and Etcd. The Control Plane ensures that the cluster remains in a desired state by reconciling actual state with the intended state defined in the Kubernetes configuration files.
explain worker node: A Worker Node is an instance of a machine that runs containerized applications managed by the Kubernetes control plane. Each node has a unique identifier and can be either a master or worker node, depending on its role within the cluster. A worker node typically runs multiple pods, each containing one or more containers.
explain api server: The API Server is the core component of the Control Plane that exposes the Kubernetes API to clients. It provides a RESTful interface for interacting with the cluster and manages access control through authentication and authorization mechanisms. The API Server is responsible for validating and processing requests, as well as updating the cluster state accordingly.
explain scheduler: The Scheduler is responsible for scheduling new pods onto nodes within the cluster based on resource availability, affinity rules, and other constraints. It uses a scoring system to evaluate potential placements and selects the most suitable node for each pod. The Scheduler can be configured using command-line flags or configuration files.
explain controller manager: The Controller Manager is responsible for managing the state of the cluster by reconciling actual state with intended state defined in Kubernetes configuration files. It runs controllers, such as ReplicaSet, Deployment, and StatefulSet, which ensure that the desired state is maintained. The Controller Manager can be configured using command-line flags or configuration files.
explain kubelet: The kubelet is an agent running on each node within a cluster, responsible for managing the lifecycle of containers on that node. It communicates with the API Server to receive instructions and updates the node's status accordingly. The kubelet ensures that containers are running as expected and restarts them if necessary.
explain kube proxy: kube-proxy is a network proxy component in Kubernetes that provides load balancing, service discovery, and network policies for pods within a cluster. It runs on each node and maintains a local cache of the cluster's IP address table. The kube-proxy can be configured using command-line flags or configuration files.
difference between deployment and replic: A Deployment is responsible for managing replicas of an application, ensuring that a specified number of replicas are running at any given time. A ReplicaSet is a lower-level resource that manages pods and ensures that a specified number of replicas are running. The key difference between the two is that a Deployment can be used to manage multiple ReplicaSets.
difference between statefulset and deplo: A StatefulSet is designed for applications that require persistent storage, such as databases or file systems. It provides ordered, unique network identifiers (UIDs) and ensures that pods are started and scaled in a specific order. A Deployment, on the other hand, is used for stateless applications and does not provide these guarantees.
difference between daemonset and deploym: A DaemonSet is responsible for running one instance of a pod on each node within a cluster. It is typically used for system-level services or monitoring tools that require access to all nodes in the cluster. A Deployment, by contrast, manages replicas of an application and can be scaled up or down as needed.
how do you secure docker containers: To secure Docker containers, use least privilege principles by running containers as non-root users. Use `docker run --user` to specify a custom user ID and group ID for the container. Implement network policies using `docker network create` and `docker network connect`. Regularly update and patch the host operating system.
difference between compose and kubernete: Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications, while Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that automates deployment, scaling, and management of containers. Compose provides a simpler way to manage small-scale applications, whereas Kubernetes is designed for large-scale, distributed systems.

what is the difference between synchroni: In GitHub pull requests, `synchronize` events occur when a PR is updated with new commits, while `reopened` events happen when a PR is reopened after being closed. The key difference lies in their triggers: synchronize events are triggered by changes to the code, whereas reopened events are triggered by manual actions (e.g., reopening a closed PR).
when would you reopen a pr and how would: You would reopen a PR when you want to re-evaluate or re-discuss changes made since it was last reviewed. To reopen a PR, navigate to the pull request in GitHub, click on the three dots at the top right corner, and select 'Reopen'. This will put the PR back into an open state for further review.
in github actions how would you add a ma: To add a manual approval between terraform plan and terraform apply in GitHub Actions, use the `needs` keyword to specify that one action depends on another. in what format does the end user reviewe: The end user/reviewer provides approval in a pull request comment using the `/approve` or `@reviewer approve` syntax.
can approval notifications be integrated: Yes, approval notifications can be integrated with email, Slack, and Teams. For example, you can use the Jenkins Email Extension plugin to send emails when a build is approved or denied. Similarly, you can integrate with Slack using the Jenkins Slack Plugin.
how does manual approval work in jenkins: In Jenkins, manual approval works through the 'Manual Approval' plugin. When enabled, it adds an approval step to your pipeline that requires explicit approval from a reviewer before proceeding. The reviewer receives a notification and can approve or deny the build using the Jenkins UI.
if jenkins accepts approve and deny but: If someone enters 'Okay' instead of 'Approve' or 'Deny', it will be treated as an invalid input, and the pipeline will fail. You should ensure that reviewers understand the correct syntax to use for approval and denial.
how would you restrict jenkins approval: To restrict Jenkins approval input to only valid values, use the `enum` validation in the Jenkinsfile. For example: `properties { pipeline { stages { stage('Approval') { steps { input message: 'Please approve this', id: 'approval', parameters: [[$class: 'BooleanParameterDefinition', description: '', name: 'approval']]] } } } }`. This will restrict the approval input to only true or false values.
if a pipeline generates an artifact and: I would choose JFrog Artifactory over Nexus for storing artifacts externally. Artifactory provides more features such as artifact resolution, proxying, and caching, which can improve pipeline performance and reduce network latency. Additionally, Artifactory supports more formats like NuGet, Maven, and Gradle.
after building and tagging a docker imag: To verify connectivity between the pipeline and JFrog after building and tagging a Docker image, use the `docker push` command with the JFrog repository URL. For example: `docker push <account_name>.jfrog.io/<repo_name>/<image_name>:<tag>`. If the push is successful, it indicates that the pipeline can connect to JFrog.
how do you authenticate and push a docke: To authenticate and push a Docker image to JFrog Artifactory, use the `docker login` command with your JFrog credentials. Then, use the `docker tag` command to add the JFrog repository URL to your image. Finally, use the `docker push` command to push the image to JFrog. For example: `docker login <account_name>.jfrog.io -u <username> -p <password>; docker tag my-image <account_name>.jfrog.io/<repo_name>/my-image:latest; docker push <account_name>.jfrog.io/<repo_name>/my-image:latest`.
what does build once promote many mean i: In an artifact-management strategy, 'build once, promote many' refers to the practice of building and storing artifacts (e.g., JARs, WARs) in a central location, such as Artifactory or Nexus, and then promoting them to multiple environments (e.g., dev, staging, prod). This approach ensures consistency across environments and reduces the risk of version drift.
how would you deploy a public facing sta: To deploy a public-facing static website in AWS, create an S3 bucket for hosting the website content. Configure CloudFront as a CDN to distribute the content globally. Use Route 53 for DNS management. Obtain an SSL/TLS certificate from ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) and configure it with CloudFront.
do you require acm when using s3: No, you do not require ACM when using S3. However, if your website is publicly accessible and requires HTTPS, you should obtain an SSL/TLS certificate from a trusted provider or use AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Without ACM, you may need to manually upload certificates to S3.
if a custom domain is required what addi: If a custom domain is required for the static website, use Route 53 as the DNS service. Obtain an SSL/TLS certificate from ACM and configure it with CloudFront. Use CloudFront's custom domain feature to map your custom domain to the S3 bucket hosting your website content.
from a security standpoint how would you: To secure a public-facing static website, I would configure an SSL/TLS certificate using AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and enable HTTPS redirection. This involves creating an ACM certificate for the domain, configuring Route 53 to use the certificate, and setting up CloudFront with the ACM certificate. Additionally, I would ensure that sensitive data is not stored in S3 buckets and implement access controls such as IAM policies and bucket policies.
how does cloudfront help with security a: CloudFront helps with security by providing a web application firewall (WAF) and DDoS protection. It also supports SSL/TLS encryption at the edge locations, which reduces the attack surface of the origin server. Furthermore, CloudFront can be configured to block common web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
how does an ssl tls certificate improve: An SSL/TLS certificate improves security by encrypting data in transit between the client's browser and the server. This prevents eavesdropping and tampering with sensitive information. The certificate also authenticates the identity of the website, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. To implement an SSL/TLS certificate, I would use a tool like OpenSSL to generate a private key and certificate signing request (CSR), then obtain a certificate from a trusted authority.
what type of acm certificate would you u: For a public custom domain, I would use an ACM Certificate of type 'Public SSL/TLS certificate'. This type of certificate is issued by AWS and can be used with Route 53 and CloudFront. To create the certificate, I would follow these steps: 1) Go to the AWS Management Console and navigate to the ACM dashboard. 2) Request a public certificate for the domain. 3) Verify domain ownership using DNS or email validation.
how do you map the acm certificate with: To map an ACM certificate with CloudFront, you need to create a new distribution and specify the ACM certificate ARN under 'SSL/TLS' settings. Then, update the DNS records for your domain to point to CloudFront's CNAMEs. The command to create a new distribution is: `aws cloudfront create-distribution --origin-id <OriginId> --enabled-variants '*' --default-cache-behavior 301`. Make sure to replace `<OriginId>` with the ID of your S3 bucket.
how do you map a custom domain to artifa: To map a custom domain to artifacts stored in S3, you need to create an alias for your S3 bucket and configure Route 53 to point to it. The command to create an alias is: `aws s3api put-bucket-website --bucket <BucketName> --website-configuration '<WebsiteConfiguration>'`. Replace `<BucketName>` with the name of your S3 bucket, and `<WebsiteConfiguration>` with the configuration for your website. Then, update the DNS records for your custom domain to point to Route 53's CNAMEs.
what is the complete request flow when a: The complete request flow when a user opens a static website hosted using S3 and CloudFront is as follows: 1) The user requests the URL from their browser. 2) The request goes to Route 53, which resolves the domain name to an IP address of a CloudFront edge server. 3) The request then goes to the CloudFront edge server, which caches the response if it exists. If not, it forwards the request to S3. 4) S3 serves the static website content and returns it to CloudFront. 5) CloudFront caches the response and returns it to the user's browser.
how does route 53 participate in the req: Route 53 participates in the request flow by resolving the domain name to an IP address of a CloudFront edge server. When you create a hosted zone for your domain, Route 53 generates four CNAME records that point to CloudFront's edge servers. You need to update your DNS settings with these CNAME records so that when a user requests your website, their request goes through Route 53 and gets routed to the nearest CloudFront edge server.
what happens when a user sends hundreds: When a user sends hundreds or thousands of requests continuously to the website, it can lead to increased latency and potential errors due to S3's eventual consistency model. To mitigate this, consider using CloudFront with an edge location cache, which can reduce the load on S3 and improve performance. Additionally, monitor metrics such as 4xx error rates and request latency in AWS CloudWatch to detect potential issues.
how would you protect the website from a: To protect the website from abusive traffic or DDoS-style request patterns, use AWS Shield Standard for DDoS protection, which provides automatic detection and mitigation of common network attacks. Additionally, configure S3 bucket policies to restrict access based on IP addresses or user agents, and consider using AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) to filter out malicious requests.
a customer has a restrictive on prem net: To connect a customer's restrictive on-prem network to applications running in AWS, use Direct Connect for high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity. Alternatively, use Site-to-Site VPN for secure, encrypted connections over the internet. Consider using Transit Gateway as a hub-and-spoke architecture for multiple on-prem networks.
when would you use site to site vpn vers: Use Site-to-Site VPN when you need to connect a single on-prem network to AWS, and want to leverage existing infrastructure such as firewalls and routers. Use Direct Connect when high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity is required, or when you need to connect multiple on-prem networks to AWS through a Transit Gateway.
where would aws privatelink fit in this: AWS PrivateLink would be used for service integration with on-premises resources, allowing them to communicate securely without exposing them directly to the internet. This is typically done using AWS PrivateLink's VPC interface endpoints or network load balancers.
what are the other vpn types besides sit: Other VPN types include Client-to-Site VPN (AWS Client VPN), which allows remote users to connect to AWS resources securely, and Transit Gateway Network Load Balancer (TGNLB) VPN, which enables secure communication between multiple VPCs or on-premises networks.
what is the difference between site to s: The key difference is that Site-to-Site VPN connects entire networks, whereas AWS Client VPN connects individual users. Site-to-Site VPN is typically used for remote offices or branch offices connecting to a central hub, while AWS Client VPN is designed for remote work scenarios.
what inputs are required from the custom: To configure a Site-to-Site VPN, the customer needs to provide their public IP address, subnet mask, and pre-shared key (PSK) or certificate information. They also need to specify the VPCs and subnets that should be connected across the VPN tunnel.
what inputs and components are required: To establish a hybrid connectivity solution between on-prem and AWS, you'll need an AWS VPN Gateway (VGW) as the central hub. On the AWS side, you'll also require a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), subnets, route tables, security groups, network ACLs (NACLs), and an internet gateway or NAT instance for outbound traffic. Additionally, ensure that your on-premises VPN device is compatible with AWS VGW.
once the vpn tunnel is established how d: Once the VPN tunnel is established, traffic flows inside AWS through the VPC routing table. The route table directs traffic to the correct subnet based on the destination IP address. Traffic then passes through security groups and NACLs for access control and filtering before reaching its final destination within the VPC or being routed out to the internet via an internet gateway or NAT instance.
how do route tables security groups nacl: In a hybrid connectivity scenario, route tables direct traffic between subnets. Security Groups (SG) filter traffic at the instance level, while NACLs control inbound and outbound traffic at the subnet level. Internal load balancers distribute traffic across instances within a VPC. For example, if an on-prem instance sends traffic to an AWS EC2 instance, the route table directs it to the correct subnet, then SG filters the traffic, followed by NACLs, before reaching the internal load balancer.
what should be verified for the return t: To verify return traffic from AWS back to on-prem, ensure that the VPN tunnel is established and the routing tables are correctly configured. Verify that the security groups and NACLs allow inbound traffic from the AWS VPC to the on-premises network. Additionally, check that the on-premises VPN device can establish a connection with the AWS VGW and that the return traffic is being routed correctly through the VPN tunnel.
are you comfortable writing terraform sc: Yes, I am comfortable writing Terraform scripts. I have experience with Terraform configuration language and have used it to manage infrastructure as code in production environments.
have you worked with terraform modules: Yes, I have worked with Terraform modules. Modules allow for reusable and modular infrastructure definitions, which can improve maintainability and reduce duplication of effort. For example, you can use the `aws_instance` module to create an EC2 instance.
how would you create 10 ec2 instances us: To create 10 EC2 instances using Terraform, I would define a resource block with the `count` argument set to 10 and reference it in a `resource` block. when would you use count versus for each: I would use `count` when creating a large number of identical resources, such as EC2 instances. In contrast, I would use `for_each` when creating resources that have unique attributes or require different configurations. For example, if you need to create multiple instances with different instance types, `for_each` is more suitable.
if you use modules how do you pass a val: You can pass a value from one Terraform module to another using input variables. In the child module, declare an input variable with a default value or no default value if it's required.
